en-C1-0.b:
Cleft sentences split a sentence to emphasise one part — very useful in speeches and arguments.

  • It-cleft: It + be + focus + who/that…: Tom broke the window. → It was Tom who broke the window (not someone else). It was in 2020 that I moved.
  • Wh-cleft: What + clause + be…: What I need is a holiday. What annoys me is the noise.
  • With all (= the only thing): All I want is some peace.
  • With the thing / the reason / the place: The reason why I left was the salary. The thing is, I don't have time.
  • Action focus with do: What she did was (to) call the police.

Common mistake: « What I need it is a holiday » → What I need is a holiday (no extra « it »).
en-C1-0.t:
Les phrases clivées divisent une phrase pour mettre en relief une partie — très utile dans les discours et les débats (= c'est… qui / ce que…, c'est).

  • It-cleft : It + be + élément + who/that… : Tom broke the window. → It was Tom who broke the window (pas quelqu'un d'autre). It was in 2020 that I moved.
  • Wh-cleft : What + proposition + be… : What I need is a holiday. (Ce dont j'ai besoin, c'est…) What annoys me is the noise.
  • Avec all (= la seule chose) : All I want is some peace. (Tout ce que je veux, c'est…)
  • Avec the thing / the reason / the place : The reason why I left was the salary. The thing is, I don't have time. (Le truc, c'est que…)
  • Mise en relief d'une action avec do : What she did was (to) call the police.

Erreur fréquente : « What I need it is a holiday » → What I need is a holiday (pas de « it » en plus, contrairement à « c'est »).
e: It was my mother who taught me to cook.
What I love about Ghent is its atmosphere.
All I need is a good night's sleep.
The reason why I'm learning Dutch is my new job.
What we should do is talk to the manager.
q: ___ I want is peace. (the only thing)
It was in 2020 ___ I moved here.
The reason ___ I left was the salary.
What she did ___ call the police.
What annoys me is the noise.
It annoys me is the noise.
That annoys me it is the noise.
The thing ___, I don't have time.

en-C1-1.b:
Inversion (auxiliary before subject, like a question) after negative or restrictive adverbials at the start of a sentence creates emphasis. It is formal and dramatic.

  • Never (before): Never have I seen such a mess.
  • Rarely / Seldom: Rarely does she complain.
  • Not only … but also: Not only did he lie, but he also stole.
  • No sooner … than / Hardly … when: No sooner had I arrived than it started raining.
  • Under no circumstances / On no account: Under no circumstances should you open this door.
  • Only then / Only after / Not until: Only then did I understand. Not until I moved did I learn Dutch.
  • Little: Little did they know…

Use do/does/did if there's no auxiliary.

Common mistake: « Never I have seen » → Never have I seen.
en-C1-1.t:
L'inversion (auxiliaire avant le sujet, comme une question) après des adverbes négatifs ou restrictifs en tête de phrase crée un effet d'insistance. C'est soutenu et dramatique.

  • Never (before) (jamais) : Never have I seen such a mess. (Jamais je n'ai vu…)
  • Rarely / Seldom (rarement) : Rarely does she complain.
  • Not only … but also (non seulement… mais aussi) : Not only did he lie, but he also stole.
  • No sooner … than / Hardly … when (à peine… que) : No sooner had I arrived than it started raining.
  • Under no circumstances / On no account (en aucun cas) : Under no circumstances should you open this door.
  • Only then / Only after / Not until (ce n'est qu'alors / qu'après) : Only then did I understand. Not until I moved did I learn Dutch.
  • Little : Little did they know… (Ils étaient loin de se douter…)

Utilise do/does/did s'il n'y a pas d'auxiliaire.

Erreur fréquente : « Never I have seen » → Never have I seen.
e: Never have I felt so welcome.
Not only is she intelligent, but she is also kind.
No sooner had we sat down than the phone rang.
Under no circumstances should you share your password.
Little did I know that my life was about to change.
q: Not only ___ lie, but he also stole.
No sooner had I arrived ___ it rained.

en-C1-2.b:
The subjunctive in English is rare but appears in formal language.

  • Mandative subjunctive: after suggest, recommend, insist, demand, require, propose, it is essential/vital/important that + base form (no -s, no tense): I suggest that he see a doctor. It is essential that every member be informed. (British English often uses should: that he should see.)
  • were for unreal situations: If I were you… · as if she were the boss · I wish it were Friday.
  • Fixed expressions: God save the King, be that as it may, so be it, come what may, long live…

Other formal structures: It is high time we left (past tense for the present). I'd rather you didn't smoke. Should you need help, call us (= if you need).

Common mistake: « I suggest him to see a doctor » → I suggest that he see / (that) he should see a doctor.
en-C1-2.t:
Le subjonctif anglais est rare mais apparaît dans la langue soutenue.

  • Subjonctif de volonté : après suggest, recommend, insist, demand, require, propose, it is essential/vital/important that + forme de base (pas de -s, pas de temps) : I suggest that he see a doctor. It is essential that every member be informed. (L'anglais britannique utilise souvent should : that he should see.)
  • were pour l'irréel : If I were you… · as if she were the boss · I wish it were Friday.
  • Expressions figées : God save the King, be that as it may (quoi qu'il en soit), so be it (soit), come what may (advienne que pourra), long live…

Autres structures soutenues : It is high time we left (il est grand temps que nous partions — prétérit pour le présent). I'd rather you didn't smoke. (Je préférerais que…) Should you need help, call us (= si vous avez besoin).

Erreur fréquente : « I suggest him to see a doctor » → I suggest that he see / (that) he should see a doctor.
e: The doctor recommended that she rest for a week.
It is vital that the report be finished today.
If I were in your position, I'd negotiate.
It's high time we made a decision.
Should you have any questions, please contact us.
q: I suggest that he ___ a doctor.
It is essential that everyone ___ informed.
___ you need help, call us. (= if)

en-C1-3.b:
Fluent speakers avoid repetition with ellipsis (leaving words out) and substitution (replacing them).

Substitution:

  • one / ones for nouns: I don't like this shirt; I prefer the blue one.
  • do / does / did (so) for verbs: She speaks Dutch, and so does her husband. I said I'd call, and I did.
  • so / not for clauses: Is it going to rain? — I think so. / I hope not.

Ellipsis:

  • After auxiliaries: Can you come? — Yes, I can. I haven't finished, but Tom has.
  • After to: Would you like to join us? — I'd love to.
  • In coordination: She came in and (she) sat down.
  • Agreeing: So do I / Neither do I / Nor can I.

Common mistake: « I think yes » (French « je pense que oui ») → I think so; « Me too » after a negative → Me neither / Neither do I.
en-C1-3.t:
Les locuteurs fluides évitent les répétitions grâce à l'ellipse (omettre des mots) et à la substitution (les remplacer).

Substitution :

  • one / ones pour les noms : I don't like this shirt; I prefer the blue one. (la bleue)
  • do / does / did (so) pour les verbes : She speaks Dutch, and so does her husband. I said I'd call, and I did.
  • so / not pour une proposition : Is it going to rain? — I think so. (je pense que oui) / I hope not. (j'espère que non)

Ellipse :

  • Après les auxiliaires : Can you come? — Yes, I can. I haven't finished, but Tom has.
  • Après to : Would you like to join us? — I'd love to.
  • Dans la coordination : She came in and (she) sat down.
  • Pour être d'accord : So do I (moi aussi) / Neither do I / Nor can I (moi non plus).

Erreur fréquente : « I think yes » (calque de « je pense que oui ») → I think so ; « Me too » après une négation → Me neither / Neither do I.
e: I prefer the red one.
Will it rain? — I hope not.
She loves Ghent, and so do I.
Can you help? — I'd be happy to.
I don't like horror films. — Neither do I.
q: I like this coat but I prefer the black ___
She speaks Dutch, and so ___ her husband.
Would you like to come? — I'd love ___

en-C1-4.b:
Hedging means softening what you say, so you sound polite, careful or academic rather than too direct.

  • Modal verbs: This could / may / might be a problem.
  • Tentative verbs: It seems / appears that… · I tend to think… · This suggests that…
  • Adverbs: perhaps, possibly, probably, arguably, apparently, relatively, somewhat, to some extent
  • Softening phrases: I'm not sure, but… · As far as I know… · It could be argued that… · I'd say that… · If I'm not mistaken…
  • Softening negatives: It's not ideal (= bad). That's not quite right. I'm not entirely convinced.

Nuance in disagreement: I see your point, but… · That's true to some extent, however… · I'm not so sure about that.

Common mistake: being too direct in professional English: « You are wrong » → I'm not sure that's quite right.
en-C1-4.t:
Le hedging (atténuation) consiste à adoucir ce que l'on dit, pour paraître poli, prudent ou académique plutôt que trop direct.

  • Verbes modaux : This could / may / might be a problem.
  • Verbes prudents : It seems / appears that… (il semble que) · I tend to think… · This suggests that…
  • Adverbes : perhaps, possibly, probably, arguably (on peut dire que), apparently, relatively, somewhat (quelque peu), to some extent (dans une certaine mesure)
  • Formules adoucissantes : I'm not sure, but… · As far as I know… (à ma connaissance) · It could be argued that… · I'd say that… · If I'm not mistaken…
  • Négations adoucies : It's not ideal (= c'est mauvais). That's not quite right. I'm not entirely convinced.

Nuancer un désaccord : I see your point, but… · That's true to some extent, however… · I'm not so sure about that.

Erreur fréquente : être trop direct en anglais professionnel : « You are wrong » → I'm not sure that's quite right.
e: It seems that the project is behind schedule.
This could arguably be the best solution.
As far as I know, the meeting is at ten.
I'm not entirely convinced by that argument.
That's true to some extent, but there are other factors.
q: Softer: "This is a problem" → "This ___ be a problem."
I'm not sure that's quite right.

en-C1-5.b:
Collocations are words that naturally go together. Using the right ones makes you sound native.

  • make vs do: make a decision, a mistake, money, an effort, progress, a phone call · do homework, business, the shopping, a favour, your best, research
  • take: take a photo, a break, a seat, a decision (UK also), advantage of, part in
  • Adjective + noun: heavy rain (not strong rain), strong coffee, a high price, a broad smile, a close friend, bitter disappointment
  • Adverb + adjective: deeply sorry, highly recommended, fully aware, bitterly cold, utterly ridiculous
  • Verb + noun: raise a question, meet a deadline, reach an agreement, pay attention, keep a promise

Register: informal → formal: get → obtain, buy → purchase, help → assist, start → commence, need → require, ask → enquire.

Common mistake: « do a mistake », « make my homework », « strong rain » → make a mistake, do my homework, heavy rain.
en-C1-5.t:
Les collocations sont des mots qui vont naturellement ensemble. Bien les choisir te fait sonner natif.

  • make vs do : make a decision, a mistake (faire une erreur), money, an effort, progress, a phone call · do homework, business, the shopping, a favour, your best, research
  • take : take a photo, a break, a seat, a decision (UK aussi), advantage of (profiter de), part in (participer à)
  • Adjectif + nom : heavy rain (pas « strong rain »), strong coffee, a high price, a broad smile, a close friend, bitter disappointment
  • Adverbe + adjectif : deeply sorry, highly recommended, fully aware, bitterly cold, utterly ridiculous
  • Verbe + nom : raise a question (soulever), meet a deadline (respecter un délai), reach an agreement, pay attention, keep a promise

Registre : familier → soutenu : get → obtain, buy → purchase, help → assist, start → commence, need → require, ask → enquire.

Erreur fréquente : « do a mistake », « make my homework », « strong rain » → make a mistake, do my homework, heavy rain.
e: I made a mistake in the report.
Could you do me a favour?
We need to meet the deadline.
This restaurant is highly recommended.
It was bitterly cold this morning.
